We analyze 96 sources---including 46 direct migration papers---across four perspectives: (1) supported software engineering activities, (2) model roles as editors or orchestrators, (3) orchestration workflows (agentless, single-agent, or multi-agent), and (4) enabling techniques including knowledge engineering, project context, environment feedback, and model adaptation. We then compare evaluation practices and benchmarks. Although 30 of the 46 studies target repositories, most acceptance evidence relies merely on build success, supplied tests, or static and model-based proxies. Moreover, compilation, visual similarity, test outcomes, and runtime behavior capture fundamentally distinct properties and cannot be conflated into a single success rate. We also identify critical gaps in requirements engineering support and in controlled comparisons of agent architectures. Finally, we discuss six open problems: application integration, platform differences, non-functional properties, generalization, attribution of gains, as well as cost and maintenance.

title: TurboFHE: An Efficient and Scalable Multi-GPU Framework for Homomorphic LLM Inference
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving large language model inference but remains computationally intensive. Existing multi-GPU FHE inference systems rely on expert-crafted parallelization plans that generalize poorly across hardware platforms and applications. We present \fwName, a framework that automatically compiles CKKS inference programs into efficient multi-GPU executables. Its compiler can split different nodes of the same computation graph at the ciphertext and polynomial level. Guided by a measurement-based performance model, its hardware-aware planner jointly optimizes task partitioning, placement, operand residency, and transfer scheduling. %Critical-path-guided rewrites extract shared computation and restructure homomorphic sums. Its backend then generates optimized GPU kernels and executes plans using CUDA graphs and selective point-to-point transfers. \fwName adapts its plans to diverse hardware configurations and FHE inference algorithms for large-scale models. On a single A100 GPU, \fwName achieves a $24.5\times$ speedup over THOR's reported BERT-Base inference latency. For Cerium's Llama-3-8B workload, \fwName outperforms Cerium's expert-crafted plans by $1.14\times$, $1.16\times$, and $1.24\times$ on 2, 4, and 8 RTX PRO~6000 GPUs, respectively. On A100 GPUs, \fwName achieves $98.0\%$, $91.8\%$, and $79.3\%$ parallel efficiency for the same workload on 2, 4, and 8 GPUs, respectively.

title: STUN-Bench: Truly Unseen Tools for Evaluating Shared Tool Experience
summary: A tool router retrieves a few candidate tools per request and lets a language model choose. Methods that share experience across organizations add past requests about each tool to what the router retrieves. StableToolBench calls some of its test groups tests on "unseen" tools, yet the ToolBench instruction pool, which retrievers and experience-sharing methods learn from, contains every test query and labels every gold tool of the two single-tool groups among them. We release STUN-Bench (StableToolBench, Truly UNseen), a split whose experience pool has no item that labels or names 172 held-out tools. Unseen here means absent from shared experience and retriever training data, not from pretraining. On the split we find crowding: experience pooled from five simulated clients, added to an index of tool descriptions, outranks the descriptions of tools no client has used, which then often drop out of the candidate list. Under the Jina-v2 retriever, routing accuracy on held-out tools falls from 0.534 to 0.278. Retrievers trained for tool retrieval lose much less, and keeping experience in a separate index recovers most of the loss under Jina-v2. The split also reverses a conclusion: with every test tool labeled in the pool and our default leak filter applied, shared experience beats descriptions alone; on STUN-Bench it falls below them. The split, leak filter and evaluation harness are available at https://github.com/<org>/STUN-Bench.

title: Revealing Semantic Gaps in Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines via Obligation-Targeted Semantic Fuzzing
comment: 18 pages. Accepted at the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027
summary: Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) prove correct execution of programs and underpin systems securing billions of dollars in digital assets. Their security depends on alignment between the instruction set architecture (ISA) that programs target, such as RISC-V, and the constraint system, polynomial equations that check the prover's record of every intermediate value (the witness). Mismatches, or semantic gaps, come in two kinds: underconstraint bugs let a malicious prover forge a proof of an execution the ISA forbids (a soundness violation), and divergence bugs make the zkVM itself deviate from the ISA or crash, so an honest prover cannot prove a legitimate execution (a completeness violation). Both cluster at corner cases such as division by zero that conventional fuzzing almost never reaches, and underconstraint bugs leave program output unchanged. Our key insight is that these corner cases correspond to constraint obligations derived from the ISA specification and the proof system's algebraic structure. We build Beak, a reinforcement-learning fuzzer in which obligations replace three random decisions: they supply inputs that trigger each obligation, reward executions that trigger new combinations of obligations, and direct witness tampering to the step where an obligation is triggered. Beak flags divergence bugs by comparing registers against a reference RISC-V emulator, and underconstraint bugs by checking whether the constraints accept a tampered witness. On six leading production RISC-V zkVMs, Beak detects 25 of 37 known bugs (67.6%) versus 5 (13.5%) for the prior state of the art, and discovers 14 previously unknown bugs, all responsibly disclosed and patched.

title: AEGIS: Evidence-Guided Set Decisions for Requirement-to-Code Traceability
comment: Code, data, and supplementary material: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23944184
summary: Requirement-to-code traceability recovery identifies code artifacts that implement a requirement, but manual review costs limit how many candidates developers can inspect. Code relations can reveal candidates missed by textual retrieval, yet can also introduce code unrelated to the requirement. We propose AEGIS, which combines retrieval evidence and code relations to construct and revise trace sets under a project-wide review budget. Grouped retrieval and semantic retrieval supply candidates. A set objective combines relevance to the requirement with structural compatibility. Local search constructs sets of different sizes, and dynamic programming selects one set per requirement within the budget. Call-context admission then compares replacements using evidence from arguments and return values in calls involving protected members, while bounding retrieval-score loss. Across 13 projects, AEGIS achieves the highest project-macro average on nine of ten evaluation metrics among the compared methods. Relative to same-corpus adaptations of TAROT-VSM and FTLR+MC, it improves F$_1$@5 by 33.21% and 52.28%, and MAP by 38.58% and 49.08%, respectively.

title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection
summary: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.

title: Software-Engineering-as-an-Artifact: From Engines to Systems That Build Themselves
summary: Software engineering (SE) is evolving rapidly as generative AI and LLM-based agents grow more capable. Yet, as a community, we risk using these new tools to solve problems that a changing SE process may no longer pose. We consider how AI may transform, and in part already is transforming, both the SE process and the systems it produces. Drawing on scenario planning methods from futures studies, we extrapolate from observed trends to a deliberately extreme scenario in which the SE process fully materializes in artifacts (like context documentation and executable skills). Such a process would culminate in SE engines that autonomously produce and update systems directly from requirements and user requests. The work of human engineers would then shift from the product to the process: they would maintain the artifacts of these engines, while the engines produce and evolve the software. We probe this scenario in scenario-validation interviews with four SE industry practitioners. The interviewees found the scenario largely plausible and desirable, and two reported that parts of industry are already moving this way; one questioned whether tacit engineering knowledge can ever be fully captured in artifacts. Even if this end state is reached only in part, we argue that reasoning about it can inform the intermediate stages. SE research should therefore take such futures into account when choosing its research directions.

title: AscendFHE: Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Ascend NPUs
summary: Fully homomorphic encryption enables cloud servers to run neural networks on encrypted inputs. In CKKS, inference requires costly arithmetic on high-degree polynomials. On Ascend neural processing units, preparing operands and reconstructing intermediate results add to this cost, while limited local memory constrains parallel execution. We present AscendFHE, a CKKS backend that coordinates Ascend's matrix engines and vector cores for bootstrapping and encrypted inference. It uses balanced-byte encoding and exact modular reconstruction to reduce vector work and packs intermediate results in the next operator's input format to avoid redundant transfers. Its two-task pipeline reuses shared buffers after their last read to overlap matrix and vector execution within the local memory budget. On Ascend 910B3, AscendFHE achieves a 4.61$\times$ bootstrapping speedup and 1.59$\times$--2.00$\times$ encrypted-inference speedups across ResNet-20, BERT-base, and Llama 3 8B over our Vector-based Ascend port of Cheddar.

title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. To evaluate this capability, we introduce RepoClean, a benchmark of 200 cleanup tasks from 34 popular open-source Python repositories. RepoClean is constructed by automatically reintroducing deleted code from real repository histories into newer versions, preserving current implementations and retaining instances where previously passing tests consequently fail. To restore existing functionality without new feature development, agents must use repository interfaces and cross-file dependencies to determine which historical code to remove and which implementations to preserve. Evaluation of seven models shows that even the best-performing model, GPT-6 Astra, resolves only 23% of tasks. Further analysis reveals that agents remove substantially less obsolete code when cleanup is not explicitly requested. RepoClean provides a foundation for systematically studying these cleanup challenges and advancing coding agents toward autonomous software maintenance.

title: DuetFHE: Compiling Dual-Lane Nonlinear Circuits for Complex-Packed CKKS Inference
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables
summary: Complex packing in CKKS stores two real streams in the real and imaginary lanes of each slot. Direct squaring couples the lanes, while squaring them separately requires two ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (HMults). DuetFHE is a GPU compiler that uses a phase transformation to square both lanes independently with one HMult. It reuses dual-lane squares in polynomial activations and the modular-reduction stage of CKKS bootstrapping. The compiler further plans ciphertext scales and reuses conjugates to sustain the complex-packed representation across stages. On a single RTX 5090, DuetFHE accelerates four polynomial activations by $1.60$--$1.79\times$ over direct evaluation on two real ciphertexts. For two-image AESPA ResNet-20 inference, it maintains packed execution across convolutions, square activations, and bootstrapping, achieving a $1.97\times$ end-to-end speedup over the fastest tested EasyFHE batched baseline on both the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
comment: 47 pages. Preregistered at https://osf.io/ms7ef. Harness, trial records and analysis scripts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24445015 and https://github.com/libredb/agent-blast-radius
summary: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs
comment: 11 pages, 11 figures
summary:
Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance.
  We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases.
  We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.

title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB). 12 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Leaderboard: https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/sudo-l7
summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.

title: NRSnooper: Enabling Real-Time Bidirectional Traffic Decoding in Commercial 5G NR Networks
summary:
Decoding both uplink and downlink cellular traffic reveals lower-layer protocol behavior, unprotected signaling, and encrypted higher-layer packets beyond what scheduling metadata exposes. In commercial 5G NR networks, however, passive decoding must overcome UE-dedicated configurations hidden in encrypted signaling, unknown identifiers of ongoing connections, and the computational demands of wideband traffic.
  We present NRSnooper, a passive sniffer that decodes downlink control and bidirectional data traffic in real time, including traffic from already-connected UEs and traffic after encrypted configuration updates. NRSnooper learns reusable physical-layer configurations through an instrumented open-source UE that reproduces commercial UE capabilities. It recovers connection-specific identifiers from ongoing transmissions and selects matching configurations through CRC-validated data decoding. A hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline sustains continuous wideband processing.
  Evaluations on a controlled testbed and two commercial networks show that, compared with using only configurations from unencrypted signaling, NRSnooper decodes 1.3x and 6.3x as many control messages and 9.0x and 17.7x as many downlink data blocks, respectively. NRSnooper also decodes traffic from an already-connected UE during an ongoing phone call and achieves real-time bidirectional decoding on 100 MHz commercial NR channels.

title: Improving Repair Agents with Cause-Chain Diagnoses
summary:
Repair agents resolve a growing share of real-world issues. Starting with the same information as a developer reading a bug report, they have to find out how the program fails before actually fixing it.
  We present FORECAST, which provides repair agents with a diagnosis of the failure. From the executions of passing and failing tests, FORECAST infers a cause chain, a short sequence of execution features, such as conditions or data flow, that explains how the failing runs diverge. FORECAST appends this cause chain to the issue an agent receives. It thus works with any agent that builds its prompts from the issue, without modifying the agent.
  We evaluate FORECAST on all 300 issues of SWE-bench Lite with five repair agents and two models, the commercial Claude Haiku 4.5 and the open-weight Qwen3.5. With the cause-chain diagnosis, every agent resolves significantly more issues. Over all agents, the share of resolved issues rises from 48.5% to 70.9% for Haiku 4.5 and from 31.2% to 56.1% for Qwen3.5. The open-weight model with the diagnosis thus surpasses the commercial model without it. The gains persist across repeated runs and for agents that already run the tests the diagnosis is derived from.

title: ParseGap: Testing What Coding Agents Authorize and What Shells Execute
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures. Preprint with coordinated-disclosure redactions (all affected vendors notified on November 22, 2026 under a 90-day disclosure window)
summary: LLM coding agents authorize shell commands by parsing a command string against a policy and passing the raw string to a system shell, so the gate adjudicates one reading while the shell executes another. We present ParseGap, a differential testing framework that runs each command through an unmodified vendor checker and GNU Bash 5.2 in an isolated container, flagging a violation whenever an approved command produces policy-violating runtime effects. Across eight production coding agents, ParseGap identifies 17 root causes across three divergence boundaries: at the parse, where an upstream tree-sitter-bash defect hides a second command from Mistral Vibe and Gemini CLI; at the utility, where every checker permits read-only binaries whose arguments write files or launch programs (9-47 of 55 cases); and at confinement, where an allow rule in OpenAI Codex CLI disables its read-only OS sandbox. Live trials across two frontier models triggered policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions). To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.

title: ReproShift: Cross-Version Adaptation of Linux Kernel Fuzzing Crash Reproducers
summary: Reliable crash reproduction is essential for diagnosing and repairing kernel crashes. Historical crash reproducers preserve concrete bug-triggering knowledge and can be reused for regression testing, bug revalidation, and impact analysis across kernel versions. However, kernel evolution can invalidate these reproducers by changing kernel interfaces, configurations, and execution paths. Migrating them is therefore challenging: the adapted reproducer must identify and modify version-sensitive behavior while preserving the bug-triggering operations and resource dependencies that define the original crash. To address this challenge, we propose ReproShift, an automated framework for cross-version crash reproducer migration by preserving bug-triggering semantics while adapting only version-sensitive behavior. Given source crash artifacts, a source crash reproducer, and a target kernel, ReproShift produces a migrated crash reproducer with same-bug validation evidence. Specifically, ReproShift first constructs a structured source-to-target context to identify migration-relevant kernel changes. It then performs constrained target-aware adaptation to revise version-sensitive reproducer operations while preserving the original trigger logic. Finally, it executes the adapted candidates on the target kernel and uses execution feedback and case-specific crash evidence to iteratively validate candidates and refine subsequent migrations. In a real-world deployment on an evolving upstream kernel, ReproShift further produces 22 upstream crash reports generated from adapted candidates, of which 7 have been fixed and 5 have received explicit maintainer confirmation. To systematically quantify its migration effectiveness, we construct a benchmark of 107 real-world source-target migration cases. ReproShift achieves confirmed same-bug migration in 57 cases, compared with 19 cases using direct replay.

title: Quantum-Annealing-Assisted Search-Space Reduction for Large-Scale Shortest-Path Computation
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures, 1 table
summary:
Computing point-to-point shortest paths in large weighted graphs can require classical algorithms to explore a substantial portion of the graph. We ask whether quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) can reduce the work required to return a verified shortest path. For a known set of queries, we select paths that share arcs. For new queries, we select a corridor and test whether any path leaving it could improve the distance found by Dijkstra's algorithm. We also partition the graph into blocks and reuse local paths between their boundaries. We compare path encodings on identical inputs using simulated annealing on classical processors.
  The comparison of exact block overlays with direct Dijkstra search covered 45 synthetic graphs and the New York road network with 264,346 vertices. The overlay reduced the number of arc inspections in the final search in 97 of 200 graph and block-size combinations. Once endpoint attachment, assembly, and reconstruction were included, every combination took longer per query than direct Dijkstra search. On a separate set of 168 synthetic graphs, tightening the flow penalty increased the fraction of trials returning a verified local optimum within 20,ms from 35.8% to 84.1% under the same annealing schedule and update policy. A cost model for a prepared graph of 16,384 vertices predicts a 1.072x query speedup over a parallel classical overlay if five local problems can be solved accurately in one batch at the assumed service cost. The practical benefit of reduction thus depends on whether savings in the final search cover the cost of obtaining and verifying the local paths.

title: Interrupt-Aware Static Detection of Deadlocks in Rust Operating Systems
summary: Rust is increasingly adopted in operating systems, but Rust's safety guarantees do not eliminate deadlocks, especially those induced by interrupts. The core challenge is to recover interrupt-sensitive lock dependencies from Rust's guard-based synchronization across function boundaries. Applying this analysis across Rust OS projects also requires specifying project-specific synchronization semantics. We present an approach combining interrupt-aware static analysis with diagnostic-guided agent auditing for detecting deadlocks in Rust operating systems. Our approach uses lightweight source-level annotations to recover project-specific lock and interrupt semantics, performs a flow-sensitive MIR-based analysis to track lock-holding and interrupt states, and reports potential deadlocks with supporting evidence. An agent then searches for relevant source code in the repository and returns a confidence assessment with reasons for each supplied report. We evaluate our tool on four real Rust operating systems, identifying 26 true cases corresponding to nine maintainer-confirmed defects. Diagnostic-guided auditing achieves 86.2\% precision and 96.2\% recall based on static analysis results, and offers advantages over the baselines in both cost and effectiveness.

title: Lightweight Spectral Subspace Filtering for Trojan-Resilient AI Inference Engines
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. Accepted at ICISS 2027
summary: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a training-free Spectral Subspace Filtering framework that detects and suppresses backdoor-induced activations by analyzing latent feature representations. Exploiting the geometric separation between benign and malicious feature distributions, the framework employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the dominant malicious subspace and performs inference-time spectral scrubbing through activation projection. This approach suppresses backdoor effects without model retraining, requiring only a small set of triggered samples collected offline. Experimental evaluation across CNN and transformer architectures, including AlexNet, ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNetV2, and Vision Transformer (ViT), demonstrates that the proposed method reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 94.2-99.8% to an average of 2.07%, while preserving clean accuracy of up to 98.54% with low inference overhead. The framework also demonstrates robustness across varying poisoning rates and multiple concurrent triggers, highlighting its potential as a lightweight runtime defense for enhancing the security and reliability of AI inference engines against backdoor attacks.

title: Useful but Unwieldy: How Software Engineers Perceive the Design of Chain-of-Thought Explanations in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents (CAs) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering (SE) workflows. As these CAs take up more tasks and responsibilities, it is imperative for software engineers to understand the CA's rationale behind its' decisions, also known as the chain-of-thought (CoT). During the interaction, some CAs are capable of showing this CoT as a separate message to users with the goal of providing transparency and explainability. However, its effectiveness as an explainable AI (XAI) mechanism for end-users in software engineering has not yet been established in the literature. This motivates us to understand their experiences with the CoT message as an XAI tool through a survey and semi-structured follow-up interviews with 36 software engineers. Through thematic analysis of the survey responses and interview transcripts, we found that CoT message is an indispensable tool for software engineers in terms of transparency, scrutability, and trust towards the CA. However, various instances of CoT messages being overly verbose, containing technical information that does not match the users' expertise, or being perceived by the users as ``detached'' from the conversation because the ``agent is talking to itself'', lead to comprehension difficulties and selective use or abandonment of the tool. We synthesize these insights to inform the design of CoT messages that support software engineers in their explainability needs.

title: Mitigating Nested GTP Attacks: A Closed-Loop eBPF Defense for 5G and Beyond Networks
summary:
The evolving cellular networks continue to rely on the legacy GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane (GTP-U) to encapsulate and route user data traffic across the data plane. Recent security research demonstrated that nested GTP-U (GTP-in-GTP) payload vulnerabilities enable a diverse range of attacks on victim users. To address this vulnerability, in this paper, we propose a closed-loop extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and eXpress Data Path (XDP) defense to detect and mitigate nested GTP-U attacks in 5G and beyond networks. The proposed framework contains three components: an in-kernel XDP Detection and Drop Module (XDP-DDM), a user-space User-Plane Telemetry Agent (UP-TA), and a multi-threaded Control-Plane Mitigation Orchestrator (CP-MO).
  We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. We also show that the proposed solution has minimal impact on the user's throughput and round-trip time.

title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

title: Relativising Integrity and Robustness: Prompt Injection and Partitioned Enclaves
summary:
Relative security (RS) judges a system against a reference system, but has only been applied to confidentiality. We introduce relative integrity (RI), which states that every behaviour a system exhibits under an attacker's influence must be one the reference can exhibit for the same trusted inputs. RS and RI each choose their own reference runs, so together they accept attacks whose leak and effects the reference reproduces only in different runs. We therefore develop a further property, relative robustness (RR), which asks the same runs to reproduce both and is strictly stronger than RS and RI together.
  We give proof methods for RI and RR and a disproof method for RI, and apply them in two domains: (1) LLM agents under prompt injection, where the reference runs the same plan with a model that never obeys untrusted content, and (2) C programs partitioned across an SGX or TrustZone enclave boundary, where the reference keeps every function inside. We evaluate the properties on models of five published attacks, a support desk, an OP-TEE HOTP token and common agent defences. Two cases pass RS and RI but fail RR: an injection that makes the support desk's model accept any customer, as one input did in the Tensor Trust game, and the simulation step of the attack on Secret Network, in which an SGX enclave reveals a transfer's outcome without committing it. Our work is fully mechanised in Isabelle/HOL, with the enclave programs verified in C using AutoCorres2.

title: FORGETMENOT: Auditing Memory Driven Privacy Risks in Commercial AI Agents
summary: Commercial AI agents increasingly incorporate long-term memory (both persistent and chat-history) to enable more accurate and personalized responses, raises significant privacy and policy concerns. Yet little is known about user privacy risks associated with memory behavior, in particular, about memory storage, disclosure, transparency and deletion control. To bridge this gap, we propose FORGETMENOT, an auditing framework for analyzing the privacy risks of long term memory in commercial AI agents. Using our framework, we collect around 3800 multi-turn sessions comprising around 6M tokens across five popular AI agents. Our results show that agents store a wide range of personal attributes, including demographics, health, and sensitive details. Furthermore, user visible memory reveals substantially less (around 20% on average) attributes than the agents store in practice, exposing a significant transparency gap. Our stealth memory injection (SMI) technique further increases the amount of personal and sensitive attribute stored in memory, raising it by 25% and 15% for Copilot and Claude, respectively. We further observed memory deletion control is unreliable, as all five agents exhibit non-zero post deletion leakage, including health and self-harm related attributes. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of memory disclosure to a 3rd-party email recipient as a proof-of-concept, as Gemini shows 31.9% leakage rate. Together, our findings reveal notable privacy risks in commercial agents memory. Finally, we discuss both design implications and regulatory recommendations to protect users memory privacy in commercial agents.

title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Classifiers for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection Using Feature Reduction
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Published in IEEE AIBThings 2026
summary: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems can improve IoT security, but high-dimensional traffic features and imbalanced datasets may reduce model reliability and deployment feasibility in resource-constrained environments. This study presents a lightweight binary IoT intrusion detection framework using an approximately balanced CICIoT2023 derived dataset, feature reduction, and comparative machine learning evaluation. The original multi-class attack labels were converted into two classes: Benign and Malicious. To reduce class bias, malicious traffic was randomly undersampled to obtain an approximately balanced binary dataset. Information Gain Ratio and Gini Decrease were then used to rank traffic features and generate reduced feature subsets of 38, 30, 20, 10, 5, and 3 features. Five machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest(RF), Decision Tree(DT), Naive Bayes(NB), Logistic Regression(LR), and Support Vector Machine(SVM), were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The results show that Random Forest achieved the strongest overall performance. In particular,the 20-feature subset achieved accuracy of 99.1% and MCC of 0.982, matching the full-feature model while reducing feature dimensionality by approximately 47.4%. The 10-feature subset also maintained strong performance with accuracy of 98.9% and MCC of 0.979, reducing the feature space by approximately 73.7%. These findings demonstrate that balanced binary classification and progressive feature reduction can preserve detection effectiveness while improving lightweight IDS feasibility.

title: LODESTONE: Linking System Events to Threat Intelligence for Evidence-Grounded Cyber Attack Investigation
summary: System provenance graphs help reconstruct attacks through causal dependencies, but these connections alone do not explain how events accomplish an adversary's goal. Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) provides the necessary security knowledge, yet linking it to execution evidence requires bridging differences in meaning and granularity between events and attack relations amid scarce labels and sparse relevant evidence. We present LODESTONE, a cross-graph alignment system that links observed system events to CTI attack relations to support evidence-grounded attack reports. LODESTONE uses a novel CTI-driven training-data engine and an expert-verified benchmark of edge-level correspondences and reference attack reports. The engine pairs real CTI knowledge graphs with provenance graphs from isolated executions. A large language model (LLM) agent recursively improves correspondences by checking execution evidence and repairing retrieval, parsing, and reproduction failures; experts independently verify benchmark correspondences. LODESTONE combines text cross-encoder and directed-graph relevance scores to extract compact alert-centered subgraphs, retrieves article-level knowledge graphs through node- and edge-level dual-softmax assignment, and uses a fine-tuned 4B-parameter LLM to align event combinations with CTI attack steps. We evaluate LODESTONE on 27 expert-verified attack cases amid continuous benign activity from real applications, using 713 CTI articles. LLM judgments aligned with multiple human experts yield an attack-step description score of 82%, and attack identification reaches 91%, versus 73% and 32% using the same generator with provenance alone. Baseline pipelines and coding agents achieve description scores of at most 57%. Human-verified correspondences further demonstrate advantages in balancing attack-edge coverage with subgraph size, CTI retrieval, and cross-graph alignment.

title: POMA: Beyond Final Flags -- Process-Level Evaluation of Base LLMs in Vulnerability Exploitation
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Benchmark catalogs, evaluator, and sample harness: https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release
summary: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from text generation to autonomous software-engineering execution, automated vulnerability exploitability verification has emerged as a vital frontier in software quality assurance and security validation. Existing security benchmarks, however, largely judge models by binary pass/fail outcomes or coarse stage milestones. Such outcome-centric scoring obscures fine-grained failure dynamics across long-horizon execution and conflates the intrinsic capability of a base LLM with external agent scaffolding. We present POMA (Pwn-Oriented Model Assessment), a process-level evaluation methodology and platform that isolates base LLMs under a unified execution baseline -- fixing task inputs, tool interfaces, target environments, feedback formats, and execution budgets -- while measuring intermediate states and transitions from runtime evidence. Evaluating four frontier base LLMs across 55 CTF Pwn challenges and 10 real-world vulnerability reproduction tasks exposes persistent capability attrition along the exploitation chain: from vulnerability knowledge to executable implementation, from client-side actions to verified target states, from failure localization to precise repair, and across iterative revisions. In real-world software, models further struggle to satisfy format, semantic, differential, and crash-identity constraints simultaneously. By pinpointing where execution chains break down, POMA provides an empirical foundation for trustworthy capability assessment and principled vulnerability-agent design. Our benchmark catalogs, process-measurement evaluator, and sample harness are publicly available at https://github.com/maple-pwn/poma-release .

title: Packing Stern into L2: GPU-Accelerated Primal-Shortened ISD for High-Codimension Binary Goppa Key Recovery
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures
summary:
Primal-Shortened Information-Set Decoding (ISD) with quadratic polar lifting recently pushed TII McEliece Track-2 key recovery to $mt=126$ (TII-228, $2{,}463$ CPU core-hours), with over $99\%$ of runtime spent harvesting weight-$(2t+1)$ codewords. Porting MiniMax's Mode-6 Stern sampler directly to one block per SM leaves $1.0\text{-}1.5\text{ GB}$ of hash tables active and stalls on global memory. For $mt \le 145$, we pack all $mt-17 \le 128$ remaining syndrome bits into one $16$-byte ulonglong2 without left-triple indices, share $G \in \{4, 8\}$ cooperative tables inside GPU L2 cache, batch $64G$ random systematic reductions per launch, and widen the shortening prefix $n'$ to cut modeled GPU-hours by $34\%\text{-}47\%$.
  Across four Track-2 challenges ($mt = 108 \to 144$), every recovered private key passes both the official SageMath checker and a standalone pure-Python verifier. Eight Modal L40S GPUs solve TII-228 ($mt=126$) in $18.9\text{ min}$ ($2.15$ GPU-hours, $3.0\times$ faster in wall-clock than MiniMax's EPYC cluster). We further recover keys for the previously undocumented challenges TII-237 ($mt=135$, $22.1$ L4 GPU-hours) and TII-235 ($mt=144$, $4.30\text{ h}$ across ten L40S GPUs, $39.62$ GPU-hours, $17.97\text{ s}$ lift), using $127$ of $128$ packed bits. These results do not demonstrate practical recovery against Classic McEliece parameters ($mt \ge 768$).

title: AgentBouncer: Defending Software Engineering Agents via Dynamic System-Call Mediation
summary: Software engineering (SE) agents can complete diverse engineering tasks by interacting with the development environment via tools that access files, run commands, and download resources. Unfortunately, the same ability that makes SE agents useful also makes them prone to performing unintended malicious actions through prompt injections, malicious tools, or supply-chain attacks. Existing defenses that analyze the agent trajectory may fail to detect such attacks, as they inspect only the initial prompt and the sequence of tool calls, but not the actual actions that are executed in the environment. This paper presents AgentBouncer, a novel runtime enforcement system that prevents SE agents from performing malicious actions by mediating, and if necessary denying, system calls that agents trigger via tool calls. The core of AgentBouncer is an LLM arbiter that judges system calls along two axes, necessity and safety for the current task. It denies unsafe system calls, and the less necessary a system call appears, the more certain the arbiter has to be about its safety to allow it. To manage runtime overhead, preseeded policy rules and hierarchy-aware caching ensure that the LLM arbiter is only invoked for key decisions. We evaluate AgentBouncer on a dataset of 340 attacks on the development environment, covering four attack vectors, combined with benign issue resolution tasks from SWE-bench Verified. AgentBouncer reduces the attack success rate from 99.41% for an unsupervised agent to 10.59%, which is 18.23-73.53 percentage points lower than competitive state-of-the-art defenses. At the same time, AgentBouncer preserves the task success rate of the agent, with only 0.25% failed benign tool calls. Per benign task, AgentBouncer adds 47 seconds and USD 0.0036 in LLM costs to an unsupervised agent, whereas the closest existing runtime defense adds 4.5x as much time and 9.6x as much cost.

title: IDSMorph: Self-Adaptive Malicious Traffic Detection through Consistency-Guided Dynamic Decision Boundaries
summary:
Anomaly-based malicious traffic detection learns decision boundaries for normal behavior and identifies deviations as anomalies. However, normal behavior varies across networks and changes dynamically, limiting adaptability and increasing retraining costs. Despite this variability, our measurements show that clients accessing the same service exhibit consistent flow structures and interaction patterns, since each service provides specific functionality. We therefore construct service-specific decision boundaries. However, variations in personalized requests make it difficult to construct stable boundaries.
  To address this challenge, we propose IDSMorph, a self-adaptive malicious traffic detection system that learns consistency-guided embeddings through two key designs: (1) a flow structure consistency builder, which constructs contrastive samples capturing consistent embeddings within services; and (2) a service interaction consistency builder, which captures local structural consistency among different clients and global behavioral consistency among clients accessing that service. IDSMorph constructs dynamic decision boundaries from the majority of similar embeddings within each service and dynamically updates them through a differencing algorithm that mitigates the transient traffic shifts within short observation windows. Experiments show that IDSMorph's detection F1 score decreases by no more than 0.12 points across network environments, compared with an average decrease of 55.43 points for prior methods. In real-world deployment with red-team operators independently choosing attack strategies and timing, IDSMorph achieves an F1 score 46.81 points higher than other methods.

title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. When the guard and the executor choose differently, the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one. We introduce this attack, tool-call smuggling, and study it across the stack. We describe six ways in which the same bytes yield different calls and build a differential testing harness that gives identical bytes to 17 pinned parser and validator configurations; most pairs disagree on some inputs, and even two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs. On tasks from $τ$-bench and AgentDojo, an attacker who can rewrite the bytes in transit cancels another customer's reservation and creates a file that the guard blocks by name, while the audit log names only the approved call. Content the model reads splits guard and executor only inside a string: ten models we test write no repeated or disguised key into the call itself where we see it, but copy one verbatim into JSON text in an argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legitimate tool's public schema and adding one field, which a note explains, gets the model to fill it, unseen by the guard, with user data. Parsing each call once, JSON text included, keeping only the fields of the approved schema, and handing it to the executor, sealed with its call ID in transit, stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack we built.

title: Conartist: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Computer-Using Agents against Multi-Step Prompt Injection
summary: Harnesses secure Computer-Using Agents by enforcing security constraints and defending against prompt injection attacks. However, we find that two core security mechanisms of agent harnesses remain vulnerable. First, consistency checking prevents agents from deviating from legitimate user objectives, while attackers can bypass it by embedding malicious actions that appear logically consistent with legitimate task execution. Second, risk auditing proactively examines high-risk operations. Yet, the auditing process itself would introduce additional exploitable actions that violate security boundaries. To evaluate above defects we found, we propose Conartist, a cascaded adaptive prompt injection framework comprising two progressive stages. First, Conartist employs a goal-pollution strategy to establish deceptive causal dependencies between legitimate user objectives and malicious operations, progressively embedding attack steps into legitimate task workflows. However, these task-coupled attacks remain susceptible to risk auditing. To address this limitation, Conartist further analyzes security-auditing feedback from controlled attack exploration to identify exploitable auditing patterns. Conartist then adaptively refines its deception strategies to either avoid triggering risk auditing or induce additional high-risk operations. Extensive experiments across five backbone models demonstrate the effectiveness of Conartist, achieving attack success rates of 32.12% on 576-instance tool use benchmark and 66.67% in the Reddit GUI benchmark, outperforming the SOTA attack by 14.41 and 29.17, respectively. By analyzing one of the most popular Agent, Openclaw, we furthermore concluded seven realistic exploitable attack patterns, which reveals that security mechanisms designed to prevent malicious actions can themselves be manipulated to facilitate attacks.

title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills
summary: Agent skills are reusable packages that extend a large language model (LLM) agent with scripts, third-party dependencies, and natural-language instructions. An agent builds a skill's arguments from user requests and untrusted external content, so a flaw left by a benign author can escalate a prompt injection to code execution. Existing studies target malicious skills or a single attack vector, and none tests whether an agent can reach such flaws. We present the first registry-scale empirical study of the supply chain attack surface arising from unintentional vulnerabilities in agent skills, over all 48,682 skills in ClawHub. The study covers two carried-over risks, dependencies and first-party code, and two agent-native ones, install instructions and credentials printed to stdout. We screen all skills by static analysis, manually review all 3,428 cases flagged by the four main detectors, and test reachability by running sampled flagged skills in a sandbox and with a live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection. First, dependency risk carries over in a different form: 49.6% of the skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE, and unlike npm packages, which mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% of them are born vulnerable, already exposed at publication. Second, few of these CVEs are reachable: agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of the affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. Third, a live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of the sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs, and the payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Hence, registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell.

title: EnvTrap: Revealing the Environment-Only Attack Surface in Embodied AI via Consequence-Blind Action Execution
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 15 tables, 5 figures
summary: As AI models evolve from text and vision to physical agents, embodied AI faces a fundamentally different attack surface. Prior attacks on embodied systems have used crafted instructions, adversarial visual inputs, and training-time policy modifications; we study environment-only object rearrangements with unchanged models and instructions. We reveal an attack surface in safety-critical spatial relations among existing objects. An adversary who rearranges objects, without modifying instructions or accessing models, can cause hazardous consequences. In this work, we propose EnvTrap, a diagnostic pipeline that constructs paired safe, trap, and null-trap (benign but misleading) embodied scenarios. We demonstrate that environment-only perturbations raise hazardous-action rates to an average of 83.4% across the five evaluated action policies, with similar vulnerability patterns confirmed in world models. On a consequence-prediction task, model accuracy remains near chance, while human evaluators achieve high accuracy. We further propose a consequence-aware defense that reduces trap trigger rates by an average of 76.3 percentage points across action policies in simulation and by 62.9 percentage points pooled across physical backends. Together, these findings link environment-only attacks to a broader deficit in physical reasoning: embodied models recognize task-relevant objects yet fail to anticipate how spatial relations change the consequences of acting on them. EnvTrap makes this gap directly testable and turns hazardous layouts into training scenarios for safer embodied action. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/INKSIR/Envtrap.

title: LaTSEC: Lattice-Based Threshold Signatures with Native Non-Interactive Identifiable Abort and Compact Per-Party Storage
comment: 38 pages. Also available as Cryptology ePrint Archive, Paper 2026/2948. Code: https://github.com/latsec-ts/latsec
summary: We present $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$, a three-round lattice-based threshold signature scheme with native non-interactive identifiable abort. Each party holds one small-norm signing share and is associated with one public abort key, against which its partial signature is verified directly, without zero-knowledge proofs or an additional interactive protocol. Prior lattice-based threshold signatures that identify misbehaving parties rely on one of three mechanisms: zero-knowledge proofs, an additional interactive protocol, or an everywhere-short secret sharing scheme in which each party holds multiple signing shares, each with its own public abort key. Compared with schemes that use the third mechanism, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ substantially reduces per-party storage. The construction uses $\mathsf{SEC}$, a recent ramp everywhere-short secret sharing scheme based on lossless expanders that gives each party a single short share. We prove correctness, identifiable-abort security, and threshold unforgeability under the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ and $\mathsf{MSIS}$ assumptions. The unforgeability proof introduces the Repeated-$\boldsymbol{A}$ Matrix Hint-MLWE problem, a new variant of $\mathsf{MLWE}$ with hints that captures the complete tuple of correlated public abort keys. We rigorously prove that this new variant admits a reduction from the standard $\mathsf{MLWE}$ problem. For 60 parties at 128-bit security, $\mathsf{LaTSEC}$ tolerates up to 6 corrupted parties, and, empirically, a randomly chosen set of at least 46 parties can sign with probability at least 0.99. Each party holds one signing share of about 14.3 KiB and is associated with one 24-KiB public abort key.

title: Ultrasound Watermark: Real-time Acoustic Watermarking against Voice Scams on Smartphones
summary: Recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS), voice conversion (VC), and AI-driven speech synthesis enable adversaries to convincingly impersonate trusted individuals during phone calls. Existing defenses often rely on offline analysis, degrade under telephony distortions, or remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks. To address these limitations, we present Ultrasound Watermark, a real-time, smartphone-native framework that protects live calls by binding speech to the caller's physical articulatory motion through acoustic watermarking. During a call, the smartphone emits ultrasonic signals and captures reflections from facial articulatory movements using only its built-in speaker and microphone. Ultrasound Watermark extracts motion features from these reflections and fuses them with outgoing speech to generate a dynamic watermark. Because the ultrasonic measurements are physically and temporally coupled with speech production, they are difficult to spoof without the underlying articulatory motion. A synchronized generator-detector architecture enforces cross-modal speech-motion consistency against replay, synthesized speech, and articulation-mimicking attacks. Ultrasound Watermark operates continuously with less than 200 ms latency overhead and requires no additional hardware. We implement Ultrasound Watermark on iOS and Android and evaluate it using over 2.5 hours of synchronized speech-ultrasound recordings from 22 speakers across eight smartphones and four real-world environments. Results demonstrate robustness to diverse attacks and telephony distortions while preserving perceptual audio quality.

title: Quantum-Resilient, PUF-Based, and Anonymity-Preserving Authentication and Key Agreement Scheme for UAV Networks
summary: We design a lightweight authentication and key agreement protocol for Internet of Drones (IoD) environments that simultaneously provides post-quantum security, hardware-rooted trust, and resistance against machine-learning-based Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) modeling attacks. Existing PUF-based authentication schemes for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) offer protection against cloning and physical capture, but generally lack resistance against quantum adversaries. Conversely, recent post-quantum UAV authentication protocols provide quantum-resistant key establishment, yet do not incorporate hardware-bound authentication mechanisms and therefore remain vulnerable to device cloning and physical compromise. To address these limitations, we integrate CRYSTALS-Kyber, dynamic challenge scrambling (DCS), fuzzy extractors, and PUF-based identity binding into a unified framework. The resulting protocol enables anonymous authentication, forward secrecy, resistance to physical capture and replay attacks, and secure drone-to-drone communication, while maintaining suitability for resource-constrained UAV platforms. We provide a formal security analysis of the proposed scheme under the real-or-random model, a ProVerif-based formal verification, an informal analysis of its effectiveness against various attacks, and a performance evaluation of the proposed scheme through communication, computation, and storage cost analyses, which show its advantages over state-of-the-art architectures.

title: Attributing Security Outcomes in LLM-Agent Evaluations: The Role of Content-Free State
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Code and data: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TARE-1217
summary: Security benchmarks for LLM agents record whether each attack succeeded and compare agents, attacks, and defenses by attack success rate (ASR). Such comparisons are valid only if the agent, the attack, and the defense cause each verdict. We show that verdicts also depend on content-free state: details of a run that carry no information about the system under test, such as the Python hash seed, the order of tools or evidence, and the scoring of failed runs. We require that this state influence no verdict (decision noninterference) and treat it as untrusted input, because evaluators and requesters of LLM-based gates can choose it. Our framework, TARE (Testing Attribution of Reported Effects), attributes a reported effect to the agent, attack, or defense only if it exceeds the measured influence of content-free state. On Agent Security Bench (ASB), runs with a fixed hash seed are identical for seven agents from four model families, yet changing the seed changes up to 17% of an agent's verdicts while the ASR moves by at most 5 points. The seed acts through the tool order: sorting the tool list instead of reverse-sorting it raises the ASR by up to 19 points, because ASB's naming convention places attacker tools first. When the same evidence is reordered, six of seven LLM judges change their decision on 17-91% of 98 proposed actions. Across eighteen agent-defense combinations, TARE's worst-case test attributes effects to two of three defenses, one of them in opposite directions on two agents, and a test fixed in advance confirms a 4.8-point decrease from the third; in the attributed decreases, 35-69% of the stopped attacks end without any tool call, which ASB counts as a failed attack. Reproducible verdicts are thus not necessarily attributable, and security evaluations of LLM agents should report the influence of content-free state. We release TARE, the ASB patch, and all verdict tables.

title: CHIP: Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection. Can OpenAI CLIP Reconstruct Images from the CPU Computational Footprint?
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables
summary:
Image inference on a shared CPU leaves input-dependent traces in software-visible performance counters and execution time. CHIP (Contrastive Hardware-Image Projection) trains a lightweight residual projector on public images to map these measurements into the 768-dimensional visual embedding space of a frozen OpenAI CLIP model. A frozen Stable unCLIP generator uses the projected embeddings to reconstruct recognizable color scenes for held-out inputs. The attack requires no physical probe, candidate image gallery, domain-specific generator, or shared cache, and elapsed time alone retains the signal.
  We evaluate full-counter, single-counter, and timing-only measurements on Intel Haswell and Sapphire Rapids. The projected embeddings achieve 0.85 ROC AUC for held-out image identification, compared with a 0.50 baseline. Exact-image top-five retrieval reaches 24% on CIFAR-100 and 56% on Unsafe-Diffusion. Across both processors, reconstructions average $1.4\times$ the baseline RGB color-palette overlap and $2.5\times$ the baseline structural similarity.

title: MirrorGuard: Defending LiDAR Perception against Passive Mirror Attacks
summary: Mirror-based LiDAR attacks passively redirect automotive LiDAR's beams to create phantom objects in the vehicle perception. Recent work has demonstrated that these attacks may cause vehicles to brake for a phantom where nothing stands. Every phantom return is a genuine time-of-flight measurement, so current spoofing defenses are not able to differentiate phantoms from real objects. We present MirrorGuard, a physics-informed defense that identifies and removes mirror-induced phantom returns before they affect downstream perception. MirrorGuard tests three consequences of the reflected path. Every phantom bearing crosses the mirror's finite aperture, its opaque surface blocks any direct return beyond it, and the two reflections off the mirror dim the phantom. MirrorGuard identifies a phantom by these cues over multiple scans and removes the reflected beams before it reaches any detector or occupancy grid. On real-world recordings of this attack, MirrorGuard removes 96.31% of the phantom's returns at 98.30% precision, with 99.99% of non-phantom returns untouched. In a closed loop with the CARLA driving simulator and the open-source stack (Autoware), a vehicle without the defense halts for an obstacle that is not present and a following car crashes into its rear. With MirrorGuard, no vehicle produces a halt or a crash. MirrorGuard runs at 59 ms mean per scan on a CPU and is a software-only solution that does not require new hardware or environmental training.

title: AutoClip-DPZO: Practical Private Clipping Selection for Differentially Private Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Differentially private zeroth-order optimization (DPZO) is a promising approach for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning, offering exceptional memory efficiency. However, its utility is highly sensitive to the clipping threshold $C$, a key DP-specific hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between noise injection and clipping bias. Existing DPZO methods typically tune $C$ by repeatedly evaluating candidate values and reporting the best result, which is computationally expensive and incurs additional privacy cost that must be accounted for under DP. Designing a practical DP procedure for selecting $C$ in DPZO is challenging because no fixed choice performs well across settings, straightforward search-based strategies suffer from poor utility and efficiency, and existing clipping-selection methods for DPSGD do not transfer well to DPZO due to its fundamentally different error regime. In this paper, we propose AutoClip-DPZO, a practical DP method that automatically and efficiently selects $C$ for DPZO. Our key idea is to avoid fine-tuning-based search by reducing clipping selection to a private quantile estimation problem, where the target quantile depends only on public privacy and training parameters. To derive this selection rule, we develop a novel characterization of DPZO error as a function of $C$ that captures both noise variance and clipping bias while remaining accurate and easy to optimize. Experiments show that AutoClip-DPZO achieves utility comparable to that obtained with the optimal $C$, while avoiding repeated fine-tuning-based search and incurring negligible additional overhead. Moreover, AutoClip-DPZO does not rely on sensitive hyperparameters.

title: ArguShield: Enforcing Minimum-Necessary Disclosure in Tool-Calling LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly use third-party tools to complete user tasks. Even without malicious intent, they may fill broad or weakly constrained fields with private information that is unnecessary or inappropriate for the receiving tool. Such calls can satisfy the tool schema and complete the task, yet still violate minimum-necessary disclosure. We introduce ArguShield, a mediation layer that intercepts proposed tool calls before execution. It evaluates each candidate value using three signals: Value Provenance, Task Relevance, and Disclosure Boundary. ArguShield releases justified values, defers values that need user confirmation, and withholds those outside the permitted scope. We evaluate ArguShield with four tool-calling models on ArgPrivBench, a benchmark of 120 tasks across Travel, Shopping, and Healthcare. Unprotected agents frequently over-disclose private information despite high task success. Prompt-only protection reduces unauthorized disclosure but substantially lowers task success. ArguShield reduces unauthorized silent release to 9% on Standard tasks and 6% on High-risk tasks while preserving recoverable task success under simulated user confirmation.

title: Bounded Autonomy: A Trust-Anchored Defense Against Resource-Exhaustion Attacks on Tool-Augmented LLM Agents
summary: Tool-augmented Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to resource-exhaustion attacks that amplify model-token consumption through persistent context amplification, large tool output amplification, and error-induced agentic loops. Despite growing attention to agent security and resource-abuse risks, a systematic defense framework specifically targeting these attacks remains lacking. Meanwhile, existing general-purpose agent defense frameworks, which address a broader range of security threats, often rely on prompt-level safeguards or coarse-grained resource limits and lack deterministic runtime mechanisms for controlling token consumption. They also provide limited support for balancing fault recovery against the risk of repeated resource-consuming execution. To address these limitations, we propose a trust-anchored closed-loop defense framework consisting of four phases: certificate-guided orchestration with deterministic handoffs, calibrated one-time node budgeting, Gateway-based runtime enforcement, and bounded recovery through a shared, non-resettable recovery pool. By accounting for both input and output tokens across all model invocations, our experiments demonstrate that the framework bounds cumulative token consumption, mitigates resource-amplification attacks, and preserves benign task utility under trusted execution assumptions.

title: WEPWAWET-CORE: A Hardware-Resident ML-DSA Architecture with Fabric-Generated, Fabric-Sealed Keys for Post-Quantum Avionics
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Spacecraft that exchange commands over crosslinks need quantum-resistant signatures, for which the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA, FIPS 204) is the standard, yet a software signer runs its data-dependent rejection loop, and keeps its key, on cores and memory shared with attitude control and payload processing. This paper shows that for a hardware-assisted signer the cost that matters is not the arithmetic but the number of times the processor crosses into the fabric, and that the boundary which minimizes those crossings is also where the key can be sealed. A gem5-supported analysis of three control granularities over the same kernels shows that only one job per signature, with the whole rejection loop on chip, takes the processor off the critical path. WEPWAWET-CORE realizes that boundary on an XCZU3EG at 300 MHz: a ROM microsequencer runs Sign, Verify, and key generation as three programs over one datapath and a banked scratchpad, and keeps the key, the on-die entropy, and the mask seed off the processor bus. The processor-side cost of a signature falls from over a second under per-kernel control to 0.53 ms, fixed whatever the number of rejections, and the fabric's time per attempt varies by less than 0.1% under a saturating workload. Under NASA JPL's F Prime with attitude-control and imaging loads, two nodes with fabric-generated, ground-certified keys exchanged 3,575 signed frames, every frame was accepted, and no attitude deadline was missed. A cycle profile places the remaining distance to dedicated cores in two serial units.

title: PLATRS: A Lattice-Based Linkable Accountable Ring Signature for Permissioned Blockchains
comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables
summary:
Permissioned-ledger cross-domain data sharing needs anonymity and accountability: an endorsement hides its author, but a regulator must identify it on authorization reuse. Existing lattice-based schemes give these only separately: public traceability exposes signers to collision detectors; linkable non-tracing schemes cannot open; threshold schemes solve another problem. None gives post-quantum security, a signer-chosen ring, a publicly comparable per-event tag, and one-authority opening together.
  We propose \textsf{PLATRS}, a module-lattice linkable accountable ring signature for permissioned blockchains. Consortium-CA enrollment binds the key returned by an opening to a registered identity. The signer chooses the ring; verification is index-free; each signature has a per-event tag any verifier can compare. Tag noise derives from the signer's tracing secret and event, so linking is one comparison for honest signatures while the tag remains M-LWE without the secret. Detection is two-tier: tag mismatch is immediate; different tags on two accepted signatures for one event trigger an opening; the authority publishes the recovered public opening component, and any member recomputes the verdict against the ring. We prove CPA anonymity from M-LWE, linkability, authority-only traceability, and unforgeability from M-SIS with M-LWE in the random oracle model. At \(N=1024\), our open-source implementation: sign 9.886~ms, verify 3.919~ms, link 0.7~\(μ\)s, open 480~\(μ\)s; signature 107.3~KiB (log in ring size); adjudication 4.867~ms. Hyperledger Fabric: 60.5 signature submissions/s at 7.87~MB/s with 16~MiB blocks, commit-bandwidth limited. Common-harness: fastest of 5 schemes to sign/verify, second in size; vs FLLL\(^+\)21, signing is 3188\(\times\) faster and signatures 133\(\times\) shorter.

title: From Dependent Ciphertexts to Sharp Bounds for Polynomial Evaluation in BGV
summary:
A central challenge in Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) is the selection of ciphertext moduli, which depends on accurately estimating noise growth during homomorphic evaluation. Choosing excessively large moduli reduces the efficiency and scalability of the scheme, whereas underestimating noise can result in decryption failures and potential security vulnerabilities. Average-case analyses have provided promising probabilistic estimates of noise growth in practical FHE computations. However, recent studies indicate that reliable estimates must account for dependencies among ciphertext errors, as neglecting these correlations can systematically underestimate noise.
  This work presents the first average-case analysis for the BGV scheme that accounts for both correlations induced by secret/public keys and ciphertext dependencies. We propose new variance estimates for the noise coefficients in homomorphic additions and multiplications involving dependent ciphertexts, and extend our framework to the homomorphic evaluation of polynomial functions, which is widely employed in FHE applications. Our theoretical estimates closely align with experimental observations, exhibiting discrepancies smaller than 1.2 bits.
  Finally, these estimates are adopted to choose the initial BGV parameters, leading to significantly smaller ciphertext moduli compared to those currently adopted in widely used FHE libraries, thus improving the efficiency of the scheme. Compared to OpenFHE, we obtain an average reduction of about 11.5% in the ciphertext modulus size, while relative to HElib, we reduce the ratio between consecutive moduli up to 23 bits per level in practical settings.

title: CyberDualEval: Measuring Dual-Use Cyber Risks in Frontier Language Models
comment: NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets track. 21 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables
summary: While frontier language models are becoming capable cybersecurity assistants, they also create a dual-use cyber risk: the same capabilities that help defenders identify and analyze vulnerabilities can similarly help attackers weaponize them. Existing cyber benchmarks measure either raw offensive capability or generic refusal behavior, overlooking the dual-use cyber assessment of preserving benign security utility while refusing assistance that materially advances misuse. We introduce CyberDualEval, a benchmark with 430 vulnerable tasks for measuring dual-use cyber risk in frontier language models. Each task is decomposed into three phases of increasing operationalization: security analysis, proof-of-concept generation, and exploit generation. To quantify the residual cyber risk, we annotate each task with a Task Weaponization Score that measures how much work remains to turn the resulting artifact into unauthorized cyber misuse.
